title: Rubio says tech outages are not part of 'systemic attack' against US
description: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed widespread concerns online that the series of recent tech outages in the past week are connected, tell
body: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed widespread concerns online that the series of recent tech outages in the past week are connected, telling reporters there was "zero evidence" of any link.Rubio acknowledged that "people are fearful" the spate of outages, which included all flights being grounded in the US and widespread disruptions to banking, Apple and Microsoft services, could be linked or part of a plot."We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."Cyber-security experts have agreed that there is no evidence linking the outages, and many of the issues appear due to updates to old infrastructure.In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage, an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours, and issues for the National Security Agency, outages affecting the biggest US banks and Apple. Every affected company or agency has said the issue was not cyber-related and not the work of an outside actor. Rubio's comments came hours after US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also addressed the issue, telling Fox News the outages were not the product of a cyber-attack. He explained "lots of institutions" are patching or upgrading systems, which has caused some disruption.Rubio was asked whether the Trump administration was concerned public fears could lead to stockpiling or a run on the banks.He said the best way to combat such fears was for the US government to share everything they know with the American people."Every indicator we have is that every single one of these events has an explanation or a cause that has nothing to do with a cyber-criminal, has nothing to do with a hostile actor or another country," he said.Cybersecurity experts say there is no evidence connecting the Microsoft, airline, and bank disruptions from the last five days.Kris Beevers, CEO and co-founder of the network and infrastructure management company NetBox Labs, acknowledged the circulating theories on social media linking the barrage of outages."There is no conspiracy here," he told the BBC."There is something more ordinary, and more important to understand: the infrastructure that runs the world is changing faster than ever, and change is risk. Much of it is 30 to 40 years old, with decades of technical debt, and it's now being asked to change very quickly."Beevers said AI is only part of the story."It's putting more strain on these legacy networks, and it's also creating real urgency around security," he said."Our customers are the amazing teams behind these networks at airlines, banking, energy, and retail who are essentially doing heart surgery on a global scale to get these networks back up and running quickly."Vice President of Threat Intelligence for Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, Sherrod DeGrippo, said: "What this week really underscores is how tightly coupled, and fragile, our core digital infrastructure is, where a single software bug or router failure can cascade nationwide."

schema.headline: Rubio says tech outages are not part of 'systemic attack' against US

title: Trump shakes hands with Putin and Xi ahead of historic talks in China
description: Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met for the first time in more than a year on Wednesday, as they prepared for landmark talks in China with Xi Jinping.
body: Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met for the first time in more than a year on Wednesday, as they prepared for landmark talks in China with Xi Jinping.The US president was greeted off his plane by the Chinese leader as he arrived in Shenzhen for a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders, which will culminate in a closely-watched meeting between the pair and the Russian president. After a carefully choreographed handshake and hug between Trump and Xi on the tarmac, the US president later greeted and exchanged pleasantries with Putin ahead of a reception.Trump and Putin are expected to hold one-on-one talks on the sidelines of the summit on Thursday, in which the war in Ukraine could be discussed.However the main focus during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (Apec) will be on the US-China-Russia talks on Thursday - the first time the trio of leaders have met together in person.A full agenda has not been made public but there have been various hints about what could be discussed, including the wars in Ukraine and Iran, nuclear proliferation, trade tensions and developments in artificial intelligence. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin and Trump have not yet held a substantive meeting, and merely greeted each other on Wednesday.Peskov also said that "no more than an hour" had been allocated for Thursday's trilateral talks between Putin, Trump and Xi.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has raised fears of a plan to end the war being discussed in the absence of representatives from Kyiv or Europe.It is unclear whether China would want this issue to be on the agenda in Shenzhen, with Beijing talking more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".China has officially remained neutral since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, rejecting accusations from Kyiv and its allies that it has been tacitly supporting Moscow, including by exporting dual-use technology used by the Russian military.Wednesday's handshake was the first in-person meeting between Trump and Putin since August 2025, when the Russian leader travelled to Alaska for talks on the Ukraine war which failed to deliver a breakthrough. Xi's personal reception for Trump at the airport mimicked a similar move by the US president when the Chinese leader visited Washington in September, a gesture Xi described as "special". In Shenzhen, a red carpet was rolled out in front of Air Force One for Trump, with a cheering crowd, honour guard, military flyover and flowers presentation all in place to welcome him.Chinese state-run news agency Xinhua quoted Xi as saying he wanted to pursue a "constructive strategic and stable relationship based on respect, fairness, and equality".Xi's greeting will be seen as a diplomatic gesture designed to begin the week's talks with his American counterpart on a cordial note.

schema.headline: Trump shakes hands with Putin and Xi ahead of historic talks in China

title: 'It was really scary': Mother describes sheltering during Russia strikes on Kyiv bridge
description: The alarms warning of a ballistic missile threat went off just before 23:30 on Monday in Kyiv. Moments later came the boom of explosions.Once again, t
body: The alarms warning of a ballistic missile threat went off just before 23:30 on Monday in Kyiv. Moments later came the boom of explosions.Once again, the main bridges over the broad River Dnipro that cuts through the city were the target and this time the Russian missiles hit what they wanted.Close to one end of the Pivnichnyi (Northern) bridge there is a large crater and in the pouring rain, water now rushes through it to the river below. Chunks of tarmac and metal are scattered around.At its broadest point, the jagged hole is about eight metres wide.The crossing is closed to all traffic apart from the occasional fire engine or police car passing at high speed. By contrast, nearby roads are jammed with cars and trucks, forced to take long detours.Anyone in a hurry to move around this city has to walk, or cycle, across the bridge, picking their way through the wreckage. In the miserable weather, that also means getting very wet.Masha and her family moved to a flat next to the bridge because they had been living by a power plant that kept getting hit by Russian missiles.Last night, she was in the kitchen of their new place when the Russians struck the bridge. She thought her windows would be blown out of their frames by the explosions."It was really scary. We had no idea they'd hit here so much. It's like we're cursed," Masha told me, describing grabbing her child and running into the corridor for protection.But somehow, she still managed to sound cheerful."It's difficult, but we're used to it. And we try to take the positive from everything. Like: we survived today! So we can be happy about that."From the damage, it looks like Russia targeted the same spot on the bridge with a volley of three missiles, aiming to keep the road closed for as long as possible. A major recovery operation is under way, with firefighters and engineers in fluorescent overalls working to evaluate the extent of the damage. But it looks like the disruption will continue for some time.Further along the Dnipro River, the Pivdennyi (Southern) bridge was also hit on Monday night, with four missiles. The metro line across it was suspended for a while, although by mid-afternoon it had been restored. The mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said road transport in one direction was also being partially restored.On the Pivnichnyi bridge, a man with a bag of tennis rackets on his back was gazing at the crater in front of him. He was heading home from the courts after he had travelled on foot to the left bank. "It is upsetting," Anatolii told us. "Then when you read the news of what our side did to the Crimea bridge, you do feel a bit better."That is because there was a battle of the bridges overnight.Ukrainian missiles hit the one Russia had built to occupied Crimea, and caused serious damage. That bridge is prized by Russian President Vladimir Putin personally, a symbol of his illegal 2014 takeover.Ukrainians loathe it for the same reason and now a section has collapsed into the sea, along with its towering arch.To many here, the timing feels significant: a blow to Putin's image, just as he wants to seem most powerful at this week's summit with the US and China.But for Kyiv resident Antonina, today is just another challenge to overcome.The 67-year-old, who we met pulling a shopping trolley through the debris on a bridge in the Ukrainian capital, was heading to see her son on the right bank, but taxi drivers were charging a fortune to go round, so she decided to walk."What else could I do?" she shrugged. "It was a very scary night. It felt like something exploded right over my head. We will get through this, but I just wish the war would end."

schema.headline: 'It was really scary': Mother describes sheltering during Russia strikes on Kyiv bridge

title: Waymo temporarily pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways
description: Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways, the company has said.The decision comes after California ba
body: Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways, the company has said.The decision comes after California banned Waymo's driverless taxis from state freeways following a series of recent traffic incidents.California's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) cited an "imminent hazard to public safety" for the ban, noting an incident this month in which several driverless Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on US Route 101.Waymo said it was working with state officials "diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations", adding that no injuries or collisions were reported following the incident on US Route 101 south of San Francisco.California's DMV said Waymo's driverless taxis presented a risk "due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present".In another incident earlier this month, footage widely seen on social media appeared to show a Waymo car trying to overtake patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing the pace of traffic on a San Francisco highway.The California ban, which came into effect on 11 November, would remain in place until Waymo "demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions".A Waymo spokesperson said: "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance."Data on Waymo's website suggests that its cars, compared to human drivers, are involved in 95% fewer crashes resulting in serious injury.Waymo currently operates driverless taxis in 15 US cities, but only offered freeway rides in a handful of those locations, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Miami.The company's driverless taxis can continue to operate on regular city streets.In May, Waymo recalled thousands of its self-driving cars in the US over a software issue that could allow vehicles to drive into flooded roads.In the same month, multiple Waymo cars were spotted driving around a cul-de-sac in Atlanta, Georgia, in the early hours of the morning.

schema.headline: Waymo temporarily pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways

title: Nvidia reports bumper results as firm says it's not reinstating Jensen Huang
description: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as it reports soaring salesImage source, Getty/Nvidia via ReutersImage caption, Jensen Huang and Nvidia's interim
body: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as it reports soaring salesImage source, Getty/Nvidia via ReutersImage caption, Jensen Huang and Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette KressByKali HaysTechnology reporter and Osmond ChiaBusiness reporterUpdated 18 November 2026 01:18 GMTNvidia has firmly ruled out letting ousted co-founder Jensen Huang return as it revealed that sales doubled to more than $100bn.In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit last week, covering the three month period just before the recent scandal surfaced, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it was "business as usual". She told investors: "We've got this."Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.But Nvidia's chair Harvey Jones said: "The board does not intend to reinstate him."   Nvidia reported that sales for the three months to 25 October rose to $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading. The company's profits also doubled from a year ago rising to $65bn. Sales from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn.The company said its rapid growth is poised to continue and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance. Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader."The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."Figure caption, Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry."It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects"."Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."The interim chief executive also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China.The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US.Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped.Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analysts' questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection."With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new chief executive will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."Michael Monaghan from investment firm Founder ETFs is among those who want Huang back in the top job at Nvidia.The Nvidia investor told the BBC that he is waiting to see the results of a thorough investigation into Huang's actions, instead of relying on "salacious allegations" made in the media.Nvidia's strong earnings are "from the machine that Jensen built" and a company tends to lose "its shine and vision" after an iconic founder leaves, Monaghan said.

schema.headline: Nvidia reports bumper results as firm says it's not reinstating Jensen Huang

title: GTA 6 reviews say highly-anticipated game is a masterpiece
description: After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.Does Gr
body: After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?According to the first reviews, it's a resounding yes.Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100, external - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.Not everyone is enjoying the glowing praise - with some posters to online forums objecting to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype." But there is no question the reviewers have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN, external branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building. "The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote, external, but he added "there are also nits to pick".For The New York Times, external one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors. Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action. But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.The graphics of the game were hotly anticipated and so far have not disappointed critics, with The Guardian, external describing Leonida, the setting inspired by Miami, as "so lifelike that at times it beggars belief".And the relationship between the lead characters, Jason and Lucia, has also stunned critics."They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim," The Guardian's Keza MacDonald wrote, adding: "I found it impossible not to care for them".Writing for Forbes, external, Paul Tassi said: "I can't say I've ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share".The Washington Post, external said GTA 6 "raises the bar at every level", while Bloomberg, external's Jason Schreier called it a "masterpiece" in his five star review."It's hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here," he wrote. "There's nothing else like it."While playing this game, I often found myself wondering how it even exists."Rockstar hasn't revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (£760m). The Game Awards - the most watched ceremony of its kind in the industry - gave players a teaser of the critical reception when its 2026 nominations were revealed on Tuesday.And despite having not released at the time, GTA 6 was the most-nominated title.It will be up for eight prizes, including game of the year and best music.The nomination of Manni L Perez in the best performance category confirmed wide speculation that she is the actress behind main character Lucia in GTA 6 - a fact Rockstar hadn't previously officially confirmed.The jury for the event is largely made up of gaming journalists around the world, who would have received advanced copies for review.Some, though, have questioned how a game that has just been released has garnered such positive reviews and award nominations.There is a view in some online forums that the hype around the game has got out of control as, with one poster commenting: "I think everyone's tired of hearing about this game - I don't even want to play it anymore."It appears so far, however, that is likely to be very much a minority view.

schema.headline: GTA 6 reviews say highly-anticipated game is a masterpiece

title: US loses measles elimination status after 26 years amid record case numbers
description: After more than two decades, the US has lost its measles-free status, following two years of record case numbers and deaths.The Pan American Health Or
body: After more than two decades, the US has lost its measles-free status, following two years of record case numbers and deaths.The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a specialised service of the United Nations, determined the US has had uninterrupted transmission of the same strain of measles for more than 12 months.Dr Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO,  announced that Mexico and Bolivia have also lost their measles elimination status, attributing the resurgence in the region to  persistent "gaps in vaccination". The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said it was committed to "regaining measles elimination status" by expanding access to vaccines.The US has seen 5,400 cases of measles this year alone, with 10 measles-related deaths, the most the country has seen since the 1990s. The measles virus - with its signature blotchy red rash - used to infect millions of children a year before a vaccine was invented. The extremely contagious virus can be fatal, and some patients can experience long-term complications including encephalitis and immune amnesia, which resets the immune system, leaving it with only limited ability to respond to new infections.The US recommends two measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) shots for children between ages one and six, which is 97% effective in protecting against the illness.PAHO, a group within the World Health Organization, revoked the US's measles-elimination after determining that the virus had circulated nonstop for more than a year."These figures are a serious warning for our region," PAHO's director Barbosa said at a news conference on Tuesday. "Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination."He added that Canada, which lost its status of having eliminated measles last year after seeing several large outbreaks, has made strides this year to interrupt transmission. Daniel Salas, the executive manager of immunisations at PAHO, said that the US and others who lost elimination status would be required to submit corrective action plans outlining how they would attempt to improve vaccination rates.US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr Kennedy has attempted to make a series of sweeping changes to US vaccine recommendations and policies. The vaccine sceptic has also frequently cast doubt on the safety of MMR shot, as vaccination rates have declined across the US in recent years. Kennedy has argued that the rise in measles cases started before he took the helm at HHS and that neighbouring countries have also seen more infections. Responding to Tuesday's announcement, the CDC said the agency and its partners were "committed to stopping measles outbreaks, protecting Americans, and regaining measles elimination status"."Together, we will encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection," the agency said. CDC Director Erica Schwartz said the measles elimination designation was not what protected Americans. "Vaccination does," she said. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities." In a post on social media, Kennedy said: "I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles." "We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," he also said. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment." The UK, Spain and Austria were among European nations that lost their measles-free status earlier this year, along with countries including Russia, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan. Nuwan Gunawardhana, an assistant professor of medicine with Columbia University Irving Medical Center, said the US losing its elimination status was "a huge leap backwards". The US was the first country to eliminate measles in the Americas thanks to vaccination campaigns, noted William Moss, a paediatric infectious disease specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Dr Gunawardhana said it took massive efforts from public health officials and clinicians to build trust with patients to increase uptake of the MMR vaccine, leading to decades in the US with few infections and deaths. But that trust has been steadily eroding since the Covid-19 pandemic, when Dr Gunawardhana said patients were confronted with misinformation about the safety of vaccines and lost even more trust in public health systems. The vaccination rate for MMR across the US has fallen to 92.4%, below the 95% level that provides herd immunity, which limits the spread of measles and protects those who cannot get vaccinated, including newborns. An outbreak in Pennsylvania has infected over 1,400 people - likely a large underestimate - and killed seven people, according to state officials. Kennedy, the health secretary, has sparred with Pennsylvania officials over how it is counting the measles deaths, with CDC declining for now to record some of the deaths in its database. Last year, the health secretary fired all the members of a top vaccine advisory panel and replaced them with his own appointees, some of whom were vaccine critics. The panel recommended a number of vaccine changes - including no longer requiring the Hepatitis B vaccine for all newborns - but those recommendations were blocked by a federal judge. President Donald Trump this year also cast doubt on the safety of the MMR vaccine, issuing an executive order for the shot to be split into three separate immunisations for measles, mumps and rubella, a move public health experts say is costly and could sow confusion about an already safe vaccine. Doctors and public health officials say the misinformation from Kennedy and Trump has played a major role in falling vaccination rates. "It's confusing patients. It's confusing families," Dr Gunawardhana said. "We need a clear message from the top."The federal government's vaccine manoeuvres have left public health officials and states to fill in the gaps, offering their own separate recommendations upholding decades-long practices.

schema.headline: US loses measles elimination status after 26 years amid record case numbers

title: Steve Rosenberg: Historic talks with Xi and Trump are a coup for Putin
description: The meeting hasn't even happened yet. But Thursday's mini summit of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping already looks like a win for the Kreml
body: The meeting hasn't even happened yet. But Thursday's mini summit of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping already looks like a win for the Kremlin. Whatever the outcome.Think back to 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine President Putin was an international pariah. Western leaders were determined to isolate him and his country over the war in Ukraine.Fast forward to 2026: Vladimir Putin has secured an historic meeting in Shenzhen. For the first time in history, the leaders of China, Russia and the United States will sit down – just the three of them – for talks.That puts Putin exactly where he wants to be: at the top table of global politics, rubbing shoulders with the leaders of the two great powers.It allows him to boast that Western pressure on Russia has failed."We see such examples in the failed attempts to isolate our country, Russia, which has faced unprecedented sanctions pressure," Putin told a business forum of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation organisation.That was followed by a meeting with Xi Jinping.But the Kremlin says the "showstopper" event in Shenzhen will be Putin's trilateral with Xi and Trump.It allows him to play global statesman, even as the Russian military continues to pound Ukrainian towns and cities, and the Kremlin continues to reject the idea of an unconditional, comprehensive ceasefire.One short meeting is unlikely to reshape the world. But it's the optics that are key. The picture. The photo-op. Three leaders, three big powers, discussing big issues.In a way, Vladimir Putin will use this meeting to send a holiday postcard to the rest of the world. Instead of "Wish you were here", he'll sign it: "Look: I'm here."But what of those who are not at the table?Among European leaders, and especially in Ukraine, there is concern that the three-way meeting might produce more than just a pretty picture, though not in a good way for Kyiv.Donald Trump has already said that in Shenzhen he wants to discuss his "favourite subject" - the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin would likely welcome an opportunity to argue its case to Trump and Xi without Ukrainian officials or European leaders in the room.Last month Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed concern that the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting might resemble the Yalta Conference of 1945. That is when the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the United States – Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt - met to re-organise post-World War Two Europe."We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4' with a redistribution of influence," said Zelensky.It is unclear whether China would want the Ukraine war on the agenda in Shenzhen. In its official statements on the upcoming trilateral meeting, Beijing has talked more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".In Shenzhen, Russia will make the most of the optics. But a diplomatic victory is not the same as a military one.Nearly five years after President Putin launched his so-called "special military operation", Russia is still struggling to win its war on Ukraine.Over this time, it has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.And the Ukrainian strike on the road bridge linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula – carried out on the eve of the summit - was a blow to Moscow's prestige. The attack severely damaged part of the multi-billion-dollar bridge built by Russia after it annexed Crimea from Ukraine.The damage is not only a logistical headache for the Russian authorities.It is a reminder that the Kremlin's "special operation" has not gone at all to plan.The Shenzhen summit may give Vladimir Putin a big stage, and a bright spotlight.It does not necessarily bring him closer to winning the war.

schema.headline: Steve Rosenberg: Historic talks with Xi and Trump are a coup for Putin

title: Palestinian woman, 72, shot dead by Israeli settlers in West Bank, health ministry says
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, A funeral was held for Fadda al-Fahidat in the village of al-Duyuk al-Tahta on TuesdayByYolande KnellMiddle East corre
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, A funeral was held for Fadda al-Fahidat in the village of al-Duyuk al-Tahta on TuesdayByYolande KnellMiddle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalem and David GrittenA Palestinian woman in her 70s has been shot dead, and several other people wounded, in a village in the occupied West Bank where Israeli settlers recently moved in, the Palestinian health ministry says.There are conflicting accounts of what happened. Local Palestinians said there was an attack by settlers in part of al-Duyuk al-Tahta, near Jericho, which is meant to be under the full control of the Palestinian Authority.According to the Israeli army, there was a Palestinian car-ramming attack on an Israeli vehicle. It said rocks were then thrown at the Israelis, who opened fire in response. It did not mention the fatal shooting of a woman.There have been high tensions in the area since a group of settlers recently set up a new outpost.They moved into eight houses in the village on 4 November after buying them, they have said, in a secretive operation. The properties are in an area where Israel retains full security control.All settlements are illegal under international law.Local Palestinians said that the events in al-Duyuk al-Tahta on Monday night began with harassment by Israeli settlers. Palestinian children threw stones, they said, and the settlers opened fire, killing Fadda al-Fahidat, who was 72, outside her home.Fadda's daughter-in-law, Nema al-Fahidat, told the BBC that she died from a single bullet wound to the head. "It destroyed her brain," she said.According to the Palestinian accounts, Fadda's son, Arafat, rushed to the scene in his car after hearing the news and collided with an empty Israeli settler car parked outside his family home, injuring settlers who were standing nearby. The settlers then fired more shots, they said, injuring several Palestinians, including Arafat."My husband, when he saw his mother, was not paying attention. He crashed into the vehicle. The vehicle was empty," Nema said."My husband got out of his car and tried to reach his mother and the injured young men. Then he was shot."She added: "We tried to gather the injured people and move them away from the settler. We brought them here. But he kept firing, firing, firing. Even after we had brought the wounded young men here and moved them away from him, he continued shooting."Nema said young Palestinians threw stones at the settlers after seeing what happened, but asked: "What can stones do against bullets?"Image source, ReutersImage caption, Medics say Palestinians and Israelis were wounded in the incident on Monday The statement from the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that "terrorists accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it", and then "exited their vehicle with weapons and attacked and harmed the occupants of the Israeli vehicle".Afterwards, it said, "rocks were hurled at the Israelis, who responded by firing in order to remove the threat."Later, an Israeli military source said Fadda was shot by an Israeli civilian and that there was no evidence that she had been involved in the confrontation near her home.Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Israel's police force said it had opened an investigation, and that officers and forensic technicians had been collecting evidence and interviewing witnesses.The Israeli human rights group B'Tselem says there has been a prolonged campaign of settler attacks, intimidation and land seizures in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, with Israeli troops now stationed nearby to secure the new settlement.Residents and activists say armed settlers walk and drive quad bikes around the neighbourhood as they threaten Palestinian residents.A BBC team saw settlers at the end of the street where Fadda was shot on Tuesday, as well as Israeli flags flying from four of the houses that they had moved into earlier this month.Image source, EPAImage caption, A group of settlers set up a new outpost in al-Duyuk al-Tahta earlier this month (file photo) In a separate incident on Monday evening, eight Palestinians were injured when they were hit by a vehicle driven by an Israeli settler on a main road in Tuqu, south of Bethlehem, according to Palestinian officials and the Palestinian Red Crescent.The IDF said the incident was a traffic accident. But the Palestinian foreign ministry called it a "terrorist attack", saying the driver hit a group of Palestinians who had gathered near the scene of an earlier traffic accident.Also on Monday, the Civil Administration - the body that implements Israeli government policy in the West Bank - announced the allocation of more than 28 sq km (6,945 acres) of land in the northern Jordan Valley to nine settlers for grazing, according to the Israeli anti-settlement watchdog Peace Now.It said handing over vast tracts of land to settlers for grazing outposts constituted "direct support for the systematic expulsion of Palestinians from their lands and the rampant criminal violence in the West Bank".The UK government announced on Tuesday that it was imposing sanctions on eight companies building Israeli settlements in the West Bank.It is the first sanctions package since Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's pledge in September to respond to the accelerating rate of settlement expansion in the West Bank, which he said risked rendering a two-state solution unviable.Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called the sanctions a "hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies".

schema.headline: Palestinian woman, 72, shot dead by Israeli settlers in West Bank, health ministry says

title: Anthropic: The seven founders about to become multi-billionaires
description: Image source, David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Brother and sister Dario and Daniela AmodeiByTom EspinerBusiness reporterIn t
body: Image source, David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Brother and sister Dario and Daniela AmodeiByTom EspinerBusiness reporterIn the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at between $70 - $78 each. If they go for the highest price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn each.So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?Dario AmodeiImage source, Finn Gomez/Getty ImagesIn 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT. He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".Listen: Dario Amodei BBC Sounds profileDaniela AmodeiImage source, Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesDario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.Tom BrownImage source, Cornell Watson/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesTom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.Jack ClarkImage source, Peerapon Boonyakiat/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty ImagesJack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.Jared KaplanImage source, Chris J. Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesJared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.Chris OlahImage source, Alberto PIZZOLI / AFP via Getty ImagesChris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum. Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain. The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.Sam McCandlishImage source, AnthropicSam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

title: Lobito Corridor: Can Trump-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo and Angola?
description: As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not th
body: As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments.She is thinking about getting around more easily.The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast. For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient."Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says.But the railway has ambitions far bigger than improving local transport.It is part of the Lobito Corridor, a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals and promote regional economic cooperation, which Washington hopes will help bring peace to conflict-torn eastern DR Congo.Under agreements brokered by US President Donald Trump, DR Congo and neighbouring Rwanda have committed to greater economic cooperation, including more transparent mineral supply chains and regional infrastructure development.The wider plan envisages linking these initiatives to the railway, which transports minerals from Central Africa to Western markets via Angola, rather than east to China as most do currently.The hope is that formalising the mineral trade and encouraging investment could help curb illicit markets that have helped finance armed groups and fuel instability.But can a railway built to move minerals to global markets also deliver peace and prosperity?The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito.Its importance has grown as demand for copper and cobalt rises, driven partly by the global transition to cleaner energy, as both are critical ingredients for all kinds of electrical components."The timing matters," says Johannesburg-based political risk analyst Wellington Muzengeza"Electrification and the energy transition have increased the strategic importance of copper, cobalt and reliable mineral supply chains."DR Congo is the world's largest producer of cobalt and one of its biggest copper producers, along with neighbouring Zambia. The US sees the corridor as a means to diversify mineral supplies and reduce reliance on China, which dominates much of the world's processing capacity.A US-DR Congo strategic partnership identifies the route from the Congolese town of Sakania to Lobito as a priority for mineral exports, while the economic framework agreed by DR Congo and Rwanda envisages connecting regional infrastructure and trade initiatives to the corridor.The project has attracted over $750m (£570m), including funding backed by the US International Development Finance Corporation and the Development Bank of Southern Africa to upgrade railway tracks, signalling systems and trains.The railway, built in 1902 under Portuguese colonial rule, was originally designed to transport goods and minerals from Central Africa to the Atlantic coast. After years of disruption during Angola's civil war, it was rebuilt and fully reopened in 2015.The US first got involved in the project under former President Joe Biden but backing has continued under Trump.At Lobito's mineral terminal, the renewed ambitions are already visible.When the BBC visited, a train carrying about 12,000 tonnes of copper cathodes from DR Congo had arrived. Workers moved the refined copper sheets into a warehouse before they were loaded on to ships bound for international markets, mostly the US.The cargo is handled by Lobito Atlantic Railway (LAR), which has a 30-year concession to operate freight services along the corridor and manage the mineral terminal.Chief operating officer Nicholas Gregoir says freight volumes have more than doubled since the company took over in January 2024.LAR expects to transport about 200,000 tonnes of copper through the corridor in 2026.For mining companies, the railway offers a shorter route to international markets."The Lobito Corridor is the shortest route for both Zambia and the DRC," to the Atlantic, says Kátila Vanessa Monteiro da Silva Neto, executive director of the Lobito Port Authority.Zambia, Africa's second-largest copper producer, also plans to connect its Copperbelt to Lobito through a proposed 830km (515 mile)-railway.But a more efficient route to market does not automatically translate into economic transformation."Joining a corridor is not the same as industrialising," Muzengeza says. "The test is not simply whether Zambia gains another route to the sea. It is whether that route helps build a stronger economy."Some Angolans believe the railway's greatest value could lie in what it offers businesses and communities beyond mining."I call it a corridor of development," says businessman Adérito Areias.The railway passes through some of Angola's most productive agricultural regions. Better transport links could help farmers reach larger markets and reduce losses."If there isn't an artery carrying products from the interior to where there is demand, those products simply rot where they are produced," Areias says.But the challenge is turning that ambition into reality.The Port of Lobito handled about 1.8 million tonnes of cargo in 2025, of which around 158,000 tonnes was minerals. Its mineral terminal can handle up to 3.6 million tonnes annually."The port already has the capacity," says Neto. "What we need now is sufficient railway capacity and rolling stock."For residents along the route, the benefits have been immediate.State-owned railway operator Caminho de Ferro de Benguela (CFB), which runs passenger services, carried a record 1.6 million passengers in 2025.LAR says it directly employs nearly 1,000 people, 98% of them Angolan."This job allows me to support my family," says Domingos Canhama, a father of four and a forklift operator at CFB."I can put food on the table, maintain a home and help support my father," he says.Muzengeza argues that the bigger opportunity is developing local businesses in engineering, maintenance, warehousing and agricultural processing."Businesses in Angola need access to the railway, not just proximity to it. That means feeder roads, electricity, storage and predictable services," he says.But can minerals and their movement along the railways line help deliver peace to eastern DR Congo, where the battle for control of mineral resources has fuelled decades of conflict?Most recently, this has seen the M23 rebel group seize control of many mineral-rich areas. The Congolese government says neighbouring Rwanda is backing the M23 in order to gain access to DR Congo's mineral wealth. Despite overwhelming evidence, Rwanda denies backing the M23.The Trump-backed agreements between DR Congo and Rwanda seek to promote transparent mineral supply chains, cross-border investment and regional infrastructure, with the aim of ensuring mineral wealth does not finance armed groups."The US wants reliable access to minerals essential to defence, advanced technology and energy systems, while reducing dependence on supply chains in which China has substantial influence," says Muzengeza, the political risk analyst"Lobito is therefore more than a railway but an infrastructure that can reshape trade routes and commercial power."At a meeting in Paris in November, DR Congo urged the US to turn its strategic partnership into tangible investments, arguing that success should be measured by completed projects rather than signed agreements."We want the partnership to support ⁠local mineral processing, electricity access for households and businesses and peace in the east," said DR Congo's Economy Minister Daniel Mukoko Samba.Even if more minerals move through formal channels, better infrastructure alone would not resolve the political and security tensions driving the conflict.There is also the question of who captures the wealth. Much of the copper and cobalt transported from DR Congo through Lobito is destined for processing and manufacturing outside Africa.While Angola can earn transit fees and create logistics jobs, much of the higher-value activity takes place elsewhere."When you export raw materials, you are also exporting jobs and knowledge," Angola's Foreign Affairs Minister Téte António tells the BBC.Areias shares that concern. "We should not export lithium but export batteries," he says, arguing that the corridor should help develop local processing and manufacturing rather than simply accelerate raw material exports.Back in Catumbela, such debates can feel distant from everyday life. For Julia, the railway already means cheaper journeys and easier movement.But its ultimate success will depend on whether it can deliver more than faster mineral exports.Whether it can also help secure lasting peace in eastern DR Congo, where the minerals are mined, remains the bigger test.

schema.headline: Lobito Corridor: Can Trump-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo and Angola?

title: Australia sandpapergate: Cameron Bancroft claims whole team knew of plot in South Africa
description: Bancroft sandpaper claims heap pressure on CumminsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith were banned for their part
body: Bancroft sandpaper claims heap pressure on CumminsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith were banned for their part in the sandpaper plotByCricket CorrespondentUpdated 5 hours agoCameron Bancroft has claimed the whole Australia team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot in explosive revelations that will heap pressure on current captain Pat Cummins.In a detailed testimony, published by the West Australian,, external batter Bancroft - the player caught with the sandpaper during the Test match against South Africa - has given arguably the most complete account of the events in Cape Town eight years ago."In 2018 not the entire truth was told," said Bancroft. "I have never been completely honest about what happened."For the past two weeks, Australian cricket has been embroiled in a debate over the ball-tampering saga following the publication of Usman Khawaja's autobiography.Khawaja wrote that the whole Australia team knew of the plot, claims supported by David Warner and Chadd Sayers. Cummins described Khawaja's account as "wrong" and "nonsense".On the day Cricket Australia announced a forum into the sandpaper episode, Bancroft published his account, explaining he was motivated by the news conference given by Cummins."The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference," said Bancroft."It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone."What I saw, experienced and lived with - not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa - is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time."Opener Bancroft was given a nine-month ban for his part in the plot.Steve Smith was stripped of the Australia captaincy and given a year-long ban, the same suspension given to vice-captain Warner. No other players or coaches were punished.In his more than 4,000-word piece, Bancroft has claimed:Sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa – the match before Bancroft was caughtBancroft had conversations with the Australia seamers – Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether the ball was "swinging enough"Before the third day of the second Test, the entire playing group and staff had "celebrations" about the effect of the sandpaperWhen Bancroft was caught during the third Test, then Australia coach Darren Lehmann told 12th man Peter Handscomb to "get the sandpaper off Bangers now"Bancroft found the publication of a joint-statement by the Australia bowlers in 2021 "deeply painful".Khawaja's autobiography and the subsequent claims made by Warner and seamer Sayers have reopened old wounds related to the sandpaper saga.Still, those connected have remained true to the accounts they have presented during the intervening eight years.The most significant denial came from Cummins, who rebuffed Khawaja's account in an extraordinary 68-minute address to the media in Sydney. Lehmann and Starc have also reiterated their denials.Now, it is the extensive detail provided by Bancroft that could shed a whole new light on the controversy and lead to further questions for Cummins, Lehmann and Cricket Australia.Cummins is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand on 9 December.A statement released on behalf of Cummins said: "Whilst we feel for Cam and everything he's been through there's nothing in the statement that hasn't been answered by Pat in his press conference."A Cricket Australia statement said: "We respect that Cameron Bancroft has told his story, and we will take time to consider his comments."We expect that there will be many dimensions to the events of 2018, which is why we have established the forum for individuals to give their version of events."We are finalising the terms of reference and will commence the process as soon as possible."In his account, Bancroft said: "I have spent eight years speaking about accountability, honesty and the lessons I learned from one of Australian cricket's darkest moments."However, in 2018 not the entire truth was told. I have never been completely honest about what happened."It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team."When I was questioned during Cricket Australia's investigation, I did not give a complete and truthful account."I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others."I did this to protect Cricket Australia's investigation and not implicate others around me."Figure caption, 'No way in a million years' the whole team didn't know - Vaughan on sandpaper scandalBancroft said his actions were "discussed" and "acknowledged" by the entire playing group at the end of the second day and before the beginning of the third day. He said he was encouraged by Saker, who has since worked as a consultant with England.The only person within the camp to express unease at the ball-tampering, according to Bancroft, was media manager Kate Hutchison."I received wraps and encouragement from members of the playing and coaching staff, especially David Saker," said Bancroft."Our media manager, Kate Hutchison, expressed her objection to what was happening."I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion."I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up."Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it."Bancroft identifies Saker as the coach Khawaja claimed encouraged him to work harder on the ball during the third Test in Cape Town. The 33-year-old said he took "feedback" from all the bowlers and wicketkeeper Tim Paine, who took over the captaincy when Smith was sacked.In Cape Town, Bancroft was confronted by the umpires when TV cameras showed him concealing the sandpaper in his trousers. He claimed Lehmann sent a message to him via Handscomb."Peter Handscomb ran out at the drinks break after I'd been caught and shoved the sandpaper down my pants," wrote Bancroft."He said to me: 'I think it's time I take that off you now.' And Pete was doing his job after Boof [Lehmanm] shouted to him on the walkie talkie "get the sandpaper off Bangers [Bancroft] now"."If he didn't know he wouldn't have said that. And if it wasn't clear enough before, then it was obvious now."In 2021, Bancroft was playing county cricket with Durham and gave an interview to The Guardian in which he said the bowlers' involvement in the plot was "self-explantory".In response, Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and spinner Nathan Lyon released a joint-statement denying any knowledge that ball-tampering had taken place."Reading that statement was deeply painful," said Bancroft."I had memories of conversations on the field in Port Elizabeth and Newlands, feedback about the ball and shared celebrations that made the statement difficult for me to digest."Figure caption, 'Cricket Australia didn't get it right' - GillespieAnalysis: Potentially the decisive intervention For almost two weeks, Australian cricket has been at war with itself over the revelations in Usman Khawaja's autobiography.But there has been an absence of a smoking gun. Without tangible, new, hard evidence, all that was left was claim and counter-claim.Naturally, the spotlight fell on Pat Cummins because of his role as a bowler in Cape Town and his elevation to Australia captain in the years since.His performance last week in front of the media, on live television, was extraordinary. For 68 minutes he took all questions and appeared plausible in his answers.In being so robust in his denial of Khawaja's account - Cummins called it "nonsense" - the skipper also left himself open to the consequences if it was later revealed he was not telling the truth.Crucially, it was Cummins' press conference that compelled Cameron Bancroft to speak out.It must be stressed that Bancroft's account is not the open-and-shut evidence that convicts Cummins or anyone else in the dressing room at Newlands in 2018.But it is certainly the most complete account we have heard from anyone involved, walking step-by-step through the genesis of the plot, the execution and the fallout. Bancroft has named names: Cummins, the other bowlers, Tim Paine, coach Darren Lehmann and assistant coach David Saker. It is, potentially, the decisive intervention that shifts this whole saga in a new direction.Whether by accident or design, it came on the day Cricket Australia (CA) announced its forum for evidence into the sandpaper controversy. Before Bancroft's account CA's action felt an unsatisfactory halfway house - not an investigation, with no guarantee outcomes will be published.What now? Will CA go further? How will those implicated by Bancroft respond? How can Cummins lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand? Could Steve Smith break a silence he has held since the publication of Khawaja's book?Throughout the past fortnight, there has been a sense that Australian cricket hoped the sandpaper debate would eventually go away. Cummins even said he never wanted to speak about it again.Instead of fading, the thirst for the truth grows, now fuelled by Bancroft's extraordinary story.

schema.headline: Australia sandpapergate: Cameron Bancroft claims whole team knew of plot in South Africa

title: American soldier arrested in UK taken into US military custody
description: American soldier arrested by UK police on suspicion of spying taken into US military custodyImage source, FacebookImage caption, Lt Col Brandon Carrol
body: American soldier arrested by UK police on suspicion of spying taken into US military custodyImage source, FacebookImage caption, Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner was arrested on 10 November ByHafsa Khalil and Daniel SandfordUK correspondentA US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia earlier this month has been taken into US military custody, British counter-terror police have said.The serviceman has been identified as Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, BBC News understands. The 41-year-old - who served in the US Army since 2008 - was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police. Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.Counter Terrorism Policing said he is now in US custody over suspected national security and espionage allegations. At the time of his arrest, Russia said it had "nothing to do with it".British police previously said he was being held in London after he was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.The day after Tyner's arrest on 10 November, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he was "unaware" of what it was connected to. "We have nothing to do with it, and it has nothing to do with us," he told reporters in Moscow.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The US serviceman is understood to have been based at Imjin Barracks in GloucestershireOn Tuesday, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said: "Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them [their American partners] to progress.""These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," he added.Tyner's arrest was the result of a long-running operation by MI5 - the UK's domestic intelligence and security agency - in collaboration with the FBI, the BBC understands.He had previously served in Afghanistan and Iraq, but at the time of his arrest was working with NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps near Gloucester - where he was said to be entrusted with sensitive information which would have been extremely damaging if leaked to Russia.Detectives sent the Crown Prosecution Service a file on the senior US soldier's alleged spying for consideration - allegations described by the head of Counter Terrorism Policing as "extremely serious."But at that stage the Attorney General's Office in London got involved. As did the US authorities.And now the decision has been taken that Lieutenant Colonel Tyner should be taken into custody by the US Military.It means he will not stand trial in the UK, but under US Uniform Code of Military Justice.FBI director Kash Patel said an army officer was in custody "as the result of an espionage investigation and the close cooperation" between the bureau, US Army and various UK partners."Together we worked to identify a potential threat to national security and take swift action," he said. "This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk."US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon said the case should serve as a "stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath" they all take."Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardising our collective defence, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served," he added.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: American soldier arrested in UK taken into US military custody

title: Kuwait says it repelled first Iranian attack in two months after US strikes island
description: Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise.The drone attack on Ku
body: Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise.The drone attack on Kuwait was the first in more than two months. The Iranian army said it had targeted the Ali Al Salem Airbase, which hosts US forces, but Kuwaiti authorities did not report any damage.It came after US warplanes struck an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to US military officials.Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates' state oil firm said a crew member was missing after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf waterway on Tuesday.The recent exchanges of fire, as well as deadlock in negotiations on a peace deal, have raised fears of a major escalation in the nine-month-old war.The conflict began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.Since then, Iran has retaliated for US and Israeli strikes by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.It has also attacked dozens of commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass.On Tuesday night, Kuwait's military said its air defences engaged "drone threats" but did not report any casualties or damage.The Kuwaiti foreign ministry condemned the attack, saying it "flagrantly violated Kuwait's sovereignty, directly threatened its security and stability, and constituted a grave breach of international law"."The explosions seemed to be coming from far away, but hearing them again after a period of calm was both surprising and worrying," Hani Mohammed, an Egyptian resident of Kuwait, told AFP news agency.Bahrain's military also said on Wednesday that its air defence systems had "intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks".The island kingdom, which hosts the US Navy's 5th Fleet, has reported four attacks over the past six days, following a two-month lull.Qatar, which has mediated in the stalled indirect talks between Iran and the US, said the Iranian attacks on its neighbours were a "dangerous escalation that threatens to complicate efforts aimed at containing tensions".The Iranian army said its drones had targeted US Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait.Later, the army's commander-in-chief, Maj Gen Amir Hatami, warned the US and its allies that it would respond more forcefully to any new attacks on Iran."If the enemy repeats its mistake... we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations," he said.On Tuesday night, US fighter jets targeted a missile launch site on Qeshm Island "with precision munitions" in response to Iranian "aggression targeting US personnel and assets", US military officials said.Iranian media reported explosions on the island but cited a local official as saying they had caused no damage to infrastructure.In a separate development, the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) said a search-and-rescue operation was under way for a missing sailor following an attack on one of its vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. The rest of the crew were safely evacuated and 11 were receiving medical care, it added.The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre reported that a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles (24km) north of Khasab, in Oman's Musandam peninsula. It said the attack caused a fire on board that was extinguished.Iran said two oil tankers and a ship carrying liquefied natural gas (LNG) had caught fire after hitting naval mines while sailing along an "authorised route".At least 25 seafarers have been killed across the Middle East since the start of the war, when the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the conflict and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.In recent months, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling through the Strait of Hormuz, allowing crude oil exports from Gulf states to reach around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts.

schema.headline: Kuwait says it repelled first Iranian attack in two months after US strikes island

title: British hacker who stole $11m jailed for six years in US
description: A British hacker has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the US for conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies via text message
body: A British hacker has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the US for conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies via text message phishing, and stealing more than $11.6m (£8.8m) in cryptocurrency from individual victims.Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, started hacking as a teenager and was part of the collective of young hackers known as Scattered Spider, which has been blamed for a string of high profile cyber-crimes.US prosecutors said the thefts had "severe, life-altering consequences" for victims and showed the growing threat posed by online crime groups.The sentence brings to an end a years-long international investigation involving authorities in the UK, US, Spain and Canada.Buchanan admitted taking part in a hacking campaign that began in 2021, when he was 19.Working from his parents' home, he and other English-speaking hackers in the US and UK targeted employees at major technology and telecommunications companies.It made them $8m in less than two years, according to US prosecutors.Buchanan and his hacker gang sent out hundreds of SMS messages to the mobile phones of people who worked for large tech or telecoms companies.The SMS phishing messages contained links to spoof websites designed to look like legitimate sites of victim companies.The group used messages like "Hi, your account is due to expire - you need to log in to your work account here immediately or you will lose access to work apps".The websites then lured the recipient into providing confidential information, including personal identifying information (PII), and account usernames and passwords.The boys and young men did it on an industrial scale with Buchanan setting up a Telegram bot to collect all the victims' credentials as the duped workers unwittingly handed over their login details.For some victim companies, subsequently stolen information included confidential work information, intellectual property, plus account access credentials, names, email addresses, and telephone numbers.The group then used stolen information and SIM-swapping techniques to target cryptocurrency investors in the United States.In the largest single theft, prosecutors said one victim lost $1.67m in December 2022.Overall, authorities calculated that Buchanan and his co-conspirators stole more than $11.6m from victims.Buchanan was also a victim of cyber-criminals.In early 2023 his online identity and home address were leaked by rival hackers seeking access to his cryptocurrency.Cyber security researchers and journalists reported that he was assaulted at his home and threatened with a blowtorch."TylerB and his group were highly sophisticated and organised but the violence he and others experienced was a sign of the troubling direction of these online communities of young hackers" says cyber security researcher Allison Nixon from Unit221B.Buchanan then reportedly fled to Canada to escape further threats before returning home.In April 2023, officers from Police Scotland searched Buchanan's bedroom after receiving a request from the FBI.Investigators recovered a device containing the names and addresses of hacking victims, along with cryptocurrency seed phrases and account credentials belonging to at least one victim.The following month, Buchanan left the UK again.He was arrested on 31 May 2024 at Palma de Mallorca Airport in Spain while attempting to board a private flight to Naples.After being extradited to the United States, he remained in custody before being sentenced this week.In his November 2023 charge, Buchanan was named along with four American men and boys in their twenties and teens for alleged activity linked to the notorious cyber-criminal collective Scattered Spider.They have all pleaded guilty too and are now serving time in jail.Two other members of the Scattered Spider group were jailed in the UK in July for various cyber attacks including a disruptive one against Transport for London that caused £39m of damage.

schema.headline: British hacker who stole $11m jailed for six years in US
